In the 7th century the Yarlung dynasty of central Tibet expanded into neighbouring regions such as Zhangzhung and Amdo, and by the 9th century the Tibetan Empire stretched from the Tarim Basin and the Pamirs in the west to Yunnan and Bengal in the southeast. After the empire dissolved, the region divided among principalities and tribal groups. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty the Sakya lama kept a degree of autonomy as political authority, while an appointed administrator, the dpon-chen, held administrative and military power.

Between 1346 and 1354 Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen overthrew the Sakya and founded the Phagmodrupa dynasty, and the disciples of Je Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school and the monasteries of Ganden, Drepung and Sera near Lhasa. In 1578 Altan Khan of the Tümed Mongols gave the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai Lama. The 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682), helped by Güshi Khan of the Khoshut Khanate, defeated the Kagyu and Jonang sects and the Tsangpa prince, and his government, the Ganden Phodrang, ruled the heartland.

Qing rule began with an expedition in 1720 that expelled the invading Dzungars. Amdo came under Qing control in 1724 and eastern Kham was joined to neighbouring Chinese provinces in 1728. The Qing sent resident commissioners called Ambans to Lhasa, and after a riot in 1750 in which the Ambans and many Han Chinese and Manchus were killed, they restored the Dalai Lama as ruler while giving the Ambans a larger part in Tibetan affairs.

Lhasa is the traditional capital, and the Potala Palace and Norbulingka, former residences of the Dalai Lama, are World Heritage Sites there. China governs most of the historical area as the Tibet Autonomous Region and as autonomous prefectures within Gansu, Sichuan, Qinghai and Yunnan. Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion and shapes the region's art, music and festivals; Bön is the indigenous religion.
timur: Timur was born in Transoxiana near the city of Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, about 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, then part of the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicized Mongol confederation. His name, Temur, means iron in Chagatai, his mother tongue. Timurid histories trace his descent in the male line from Tumbinai Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, but no written evidence from his own lifetime links him directly to Genghis Khan. By about 1360 he had become a military leader whose troops were mostly Turkic tribesmen, and he campaigned in Transoxiana with the Khan of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur reduced the Chagatai khans to figureheads and ruled in their name. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, Mongol tradition denied him the title of khan, so he used the title of amir and set up a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. His first campaigns took Khwarazm and Urgench, and in 1383 he began his conquest of Persia. When Herat did not surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its citizens.

In 1398 Timur invaded the Indian subcontinent, where the Tughlaq dynasty's Delhi Sultanate had declined and most provincial governors had asserted their independence. He crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 with a force of 90,000 and sacked Tulamba, massacring its inhabitants. Before the battle for Delhi on 17 December 1398 he slaughtered some 100,000 captives, fearing that they might revolt. In the following years he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, and had Ming envoys detained. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions.

In December 1404 Timur began a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill beyond the Syr Daria and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405. He had outlived two chosen heirs, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and on his deathbed named Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. A civil war among his descendants followed, and his youngest son Shah Rukh took the throne only in 1409.

His legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him, while Baghdad, Damascus, Delhi and other cities were sacked and their people massacred. He keeps a positive image in Muslim Central Asia and is vilified in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India. Two Zafarnamas written under Timurid patronage present him favourably, while the Arabic chronicle of Ahmad ibn Arabshah is far less so.
tin: Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn, from the Latin stannum, and atomic number 50. It is a soft, silvery-white, malleable metal that can be cut with little force, and a bent bar of tin makes a crackling sound known as the tin cry, caused by the twinning of its crystals. It resists corrosion from water. It does not occur as the native element but is extracted from ores, chiefly cassiterite, the only commercially important source, which is almost always associated with granite.

The word tin is shared among the Germanic languages and traces back to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic form; cognates include German Zinn, Swedish tenn and Dutch tin. The Latin name stannum or stagnum originally meant an alloy of silver and lead, and came to mean tin in the fourth century. The earlier Latin word was plumbum candidum, or white lead. The origin of stannum is unknown and may be pre-Indo-European.

Tin extraction and use can be dated to the beginnings of the Bronze Age around 3000 BCE. The earliest bronze objects had a tin or arsenic content of under 2 per cent and are believed to be the result of unintentional alloying. Adding a second metal to copper increases its hardness, lowers its melting temperature and gives a more fluid melt, which allowed the more complex shapes cast in closed moulds of the Bronze Age.

Arsenical bronze appears first in the Near East, where arsenic is commonly found with copper ore, but its health risks were quickly realised, and the quest for sources of the much less hazardous tin began early in the Bronze Age. This created a demand for rare tin and a trade network linking distant sources of tin to the markets of Bronze Age cultures. The first tin alloy used on a large scale was bronze, of one eighth tin and seven eighths copper; after 600 BCE pure metallic tin was produced. Pewter, an alloy of 85 to 90 per cent tin, has been used for flatware since the Bronze Age.
tirana: Tirana lies on the Plain of Tirana in the centre of Albania, between Mount Dajti to the east, hills to the south and a valley to the north that overlooks the Adriatic Sea. Its average altitude is about 110 metres. The Tiranë and Lanë rivers flow through the city. Dajti National Park lies on the mountain above it, with forests of pine, oak and beech, and the city's mountains are a popular retreat in winter, when snow often covers them although the city itself rarely receives it.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with the earliest recognised reference at the Cave of Pëllumbas, of the Palaeolithic period. Illyrians were its first population and most likely formed the core of the Illyrian kingdom of the Taulantii. After the Illyrian Wars the Romans integrated the area into their empire. The oldest surviving find from that period is a Roman house of the 3rd century, later turned into a church with a mosaic floor. A castle, possibly known as Tirkan, was built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and was restored by Ahmed Pasha Toptani in the 18th century.

Tirana appears in Venetian documents of the 1350s and in 1418. The first Ottoman land registrations of 1431–32 record 60 inhabited areas with nearly 2,028 houses and 7,300 inhabitants. In 1510 Marin Barleti, in his biography of Skanderbeg, called it a small village, distinguishing Little Tirana from Great Tirana. The town was founded in 1614 by the Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, who built the Old Mosque, a small commercial centre and a hammam. Some sources describe a bazaar with watermills already existing before 1614. In the 16th century craftsmen made silk and cotton fabrics, leather, ceramics and metal artefacts. The Et'hem Bey Mosque was completed in 1821.

The city was fairly unimportant until the 20th century, when the Congress of Lushnjë proclaimed it the capital of Albania following the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 1912. Its present appearance was shaped by two totalitarian regimes: Mussolini's, whose architects Florestano Di Fausto and Armando Brasini designed the ministry buildings, and Enver Hoxha's afterwards. The population tenfolded between 1820 and 1955, and it grew faster after the fall of communism.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania and seat of its government, parliament and highest courts. The centre from the University of Tirana's Mother Teresa Square to Skanderbeg Square was declared a protected cultural area in 2000. The 2023 census counted 598,176 residents in the municipality. The airport is named after Mother Teresa.
togo: Togo is a small tropical country of 56,785 square kilometres, less than 115 kilometres wide between Ghana and Benin. It extends north from the Gulf of Guinea, where its coast is 56 kilometres long and consists of lagoons with sandy beaches, to the border with Burkina Faso. The south has a savannah and woodland plateau reaching a coastal plain with lagoons and marshes, the centre is hilly, and the north is rolling savannah. The highest mountain is Mont Agou at 986 metres, and the longest river is the Mono, at 400 kilometres.

The name Togo means 'by the water' or 'behind the sea', from the Ewe words to, 'water', and go, 'shore'. It originally referred only to the town of Togo, now Togoville, and the Germans later extended it to the whole country.

Archaeological finds indicate that societies in the area could produce pottery and process iron. Between the 11th and 16th centuries the Ewe entered the area from the west, and the Mina and Gun from the east, and most settled on the coast. The Atlantic slave trade began in the 16th century. For the next two hundred years the coastal region was a trading centre for Europeans in search of slaves, which earned Togo and the surrounding region the name the Slave Coast.

In 1884 a paper was forcibly signed at Togoville with King Mlapa III, whereby Germany claimed a protectorate over a stretch of coast and gradually extended its control inland. In 1905 this became the German colony of Togoland. The local population was forced to work, to cultivate cotton, coffee and cocoa, and to pay taxes, and a railway and the port of Lomé were built for export.

Britain and France invaded in August 1914, and German forces surrendered on 26 August. The territory was partitioned into British and French zones, which on 20 July 1922 became League of Nations mandates. French Togoland became an autonomous republic in 1956, and British Togoland voted to join the Gold Coast, as part of Ghana, in 1957. Togo became independent from France in 1960.

Togo is the Togolese Republic, with its capital, Lomé, on the Gulf of Guinea. French is the official language, and Kabiye and Ewe are national languages. The population is about 8 million, with some 40 ethnic groups, of which the Ewe in the south are the most numerous. Culture draws on Ewe and Mina traditions in the south, including the creator god Mawu and the vodun, and on Kabye and Tem traditions in the north, including the Evala wrestling initiation rite.
tokelau: Tokelau consists of three tropical coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, with a combined land area of about 10 square kilometres, between latitudes 8 and 10 degrees south, about midway between Hawaii and New Zealand and some 500 kilometres north of Samoa. The highest point is just 5 metres above sea level, and the islands lie in the Pacific tropical cyclone belt. Swains Island (Olohega), culturally and geographically part of the same archipelago, has been under United States control since about 1900 and is administered as part of American Samoa. The name is a Tokelauan word meaning north wind; European explorers called the group the Union Islands, and it was shortened to Tokelau on 9 December 1976.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the atolls were settled about 1,000 years ago from Samoa. The three atolls functioned separately in politics while keeping social and linguistic cohesion, governed by chiefly clans, with occasional wars between atolls as well as intermarriage; Fakaofo held some dominion over Atafu and Nukunonu. Life was subsistence-based, relying mainly on fish and coconut.

Commodore John Byron sighted Atafu on 24 June 1765, and Captain Edward Edwards visited it in June 1791 in search of the Bounty mutineers. In 1877 an Order in Council placed the islands under United Kingdom protection, and in June 1889 Commander C. F. Oldham of HMS Egeria raised the Union Flag on each atoll. They were annexed on 29 February 1916 and included in the Gilbert Islands. They were placed under the Governor-General of New Zealand in 1925, and New Zealand took over administration on 11 February 1926, though sovereignty remained with the United Kingdom.

Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand, whose King is its head of state, and both governments call it a nation. About 2,500 people live there, and some 94 per cent speak Tokelauan as their first language. Since 1993 the territory has elected its own head of government, the Ulu-o-Tokelau, a post that rotates among the faipule of the three atolls, and the basis of its system is the Tokelau Islands Act 1948. Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for further self-determination.
toronto: Toronto stands on a harbour on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario, on a broad sloping plateau interspersed with rivers, deep ravines and urban forest. The city covers 631 square kilometres and has a 46-kilometre waterfront. The Toronto Islands and Port Lands extend into the lake and shelter the harbour south of downtown. The name was recorded in many spellings. The early form Taronto referred to the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, which the Mohawk called tkaronto, meaning where there are trees standing in the water, a name recorded as early as 1615 by Samuel de Champlain.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the area for more than 10,000 years. The Wendat, an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people, farmed it for centuries before European contact, until the Haudenosaunee invaded and massacred them between 1648 and 1650. By the 1660s the Haudenosaunee had two villages in what is now Toronto, Ganatsekwyagon on the Rouge River and Teiaiagon on the Humber River. By 1701 the Mississaugas, an Anishinaabe-speaking people from northern Ontario, had displaced them at the end of the Beaver Wars. A portage route from Lake Ontario to Lake Huron, the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, led to the wide use of the name.

French traders founded Fort Rouillé in 1750 but abandoned it in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. The British defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, and in 1763 the area became part of the colony of Quebec. After the broadly disputed Toronto Purchase, in which the Mississaugas surrendered the area to the British Crown, the British established the town of York in 1793 and later made it the capital of Upper Canada.

During the War of 1812 York was the site of the Battle of York, which caused heavy damage and a two-week occupation by American troops. It was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834. In 1867, at Canadian Confederation, it became the capital of the province of Ontario. The city grew beyond its original limits by annexation and amalgamation, reaching its present area in 1998. The completion of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 gave ships access to the Great Lakes from the Atlantic.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and the most populous city in Canada, with 2,794,356 people at the 2021 census. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, over 200 ethnic origins are represented, and more than 160 languages are spoken. It is governed by a mayor and a unicameral city council of 25 councillors. It is Canada's largest financial centre and the home of the Toronto Stock Exchange, and of institutions such as the National Ballet of Canada, the Canadian Opera Company and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra.
toulouse: Toulouse lies on the banks of the Garonne, 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, 230 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean and 680 kilometres from Paris, on the axis of communication between the two seas. The Garonne valley has been a central point for trade between the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic since at least the Iron Age. The historical name of the city, Tolosa, and that of its inhabitants, the Tolosates, first recorded in the 2nd century BCE, is of unknown meaning or origin, and has been connected with the Gaulish Volcae Tectosages and, by others, with a root meaning little hill.

Charlemagne created the county of Toulouse in 778 to guard the border of Muslim Spain. The disintegration of the kingdom of Aquitaine and the weakness of royal power in the following centuries led to the de facto independence of the county. The treaty of 1229 made Toulouse subordinate to the kingdom of France, and when Joan of Toulouse and her husband Alphonse of Poitiers died without heirs in 1271 the city had no count and was annexed to the royal domain. Royal officers settled in the city, trade and crafts grew, and in 1298 King Philip the Fair eased the ennobling of the capitouls, whose annually renewed council was increasingly made up of rich merchants.

The University of Toulouse was founded in 1229. In the 16th century the woad trade brought merchants of international stature to the city, and the Parlement of Toulouse made it the judicial capital of much of the south of France.

On 10 April 1814 Wellington's Hispanic-British troops fought the French under Marshal Soult at the Battle of Toulouse, four days after Napoleon's surrender, though neither army yet knew of it; it was the last Franco-British battle on French territory. In the First World War the city, sheltered from attack, gained chemical industries and aviation workshops, which began its aeronautical tradition and gave rise to the airmail company Aéropostale.

Toulouse is the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and of the Occitania region, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries in 2023. Its architecture of pinkish terracotta brick has earned it the name La Ville rose. The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe, and the former hospital Hôtel-Dieu Saint-Jacques are World Heritage Sites for their place on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, as is the Canal du Midi, which begins in the city. Toulouse is the centre of the European aerospace industry, with the headquarters of Airbus, and its rugby club, Stade Toulousain, is among the most successful in Europe.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
trigonometry: The word comes from the Ancient Greek trigonon, "triangle", and metron, "measure". Sumerian astronomers studied angle measure, dividing the circle into 360 degrees. They and the later Babylonians studied the ratios of the sides of similar triangles and found some of their properties, but did not make a systematic method for finding the sides and angles of triangles. The ancient Nubians used a similar method. In the 3rd century BCE Hellenistic mathematicians such as Euclid and Archimedes studied chords and inscribed angles in circles and proved theorems equivalent to modern trigonometric formulae, though they presented them geometrically rather than algebraically.

Hipparchus of Nicaea gave the first tables of chords in 140 BCE, and in the 2nd century CE Ptolemy constructed detailed tables in Book 1 of his Almagest. Ptolemy's treatise stayed in use for calculations in astronomy for the next 1,200 years in the Byzantine, Islamic and later Western European worlds.

Trigonometry relates the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its side lengths. The sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse, the cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and the tangent the ratio of the opposite to the adjacent side. Their reciprocals are the cosecant, secant and cotangent. With the laws of sines and cosines one can find the remaining sides and angles of any triangle once enough of them are known. Spherical trigonometry applies the same ideas to triangles on a sphere, and was long used to locate the sun, moon and stars and to predict eclipses.

The modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Surya Siddhanta, and Aryabhata documented its properties in the 5th century CE. Medieval Islamic mathematicians translated and expanded Greek and Indian works. Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi made the first table of cotangents in 830 CE, and by the 10th century Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani used all six functions, with sine tables in steps of a quarter of a degree.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was the first to treat trigonometry as a discipline independent of astronomy, and in the 14th century Madhava of Sangamagrama developed infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Knowledge reached Western Europe through Latin translations of the Almagest and the works of al-Battani and al-Tusi. Regiomontanus wrote De Triangulis in the 15th century, and Copernicus devoted two chapters of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to the basics. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus first used the word trigonometry in his Trigonometria of 1595, and Gemma Frisius described the method of triangulation still used in surveying.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters. The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
tunisia: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of north-west Africa, bordered by Algeria to the west and south-west and Libya to the south-east. It covers 163,610 square kilometres and has a coastline of about 1,300 kilometres. The Dorsal, the eastern extension of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country north-eastward; north of it lies the Tell, a region of low hills and plains. The Sahel, a coastal plain on the east, is among the world's premier areas of olive cultivation, and much of the south is semi-arid and desert. Tunis, the capital, stands on a hill slope above the lake of Tunis.

Tunisia was inhabited by Berber tribes at the beginning of recorded history. Phoenicians began settling the coast from as early as the 12th century BCE, at Bizerte and Utica. Carthage, founded in the 9th century BCE, became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean after wars with the Greek city-states of Sicily. According to the Greek writer Timaeus of Tauromenium, Dido of Tyre founded it in 814 BCE, though this is regarded as legend. Its people worshipped Baal and Tanit. After the Second Punic War, in which Hannibal invaded Italy, Carthage was a client state of Rome until it was conquered in 146 BCE and made the province of Africa.

Arab Muslims conquered Tunisia in the 7th century CE, and the migration of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes in the 11th and 12th centuries accelerated the process, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabised. The Ottoman Empire took control in 1546 and held it until the French conquest of 1881. Tunisia became independent as the Tunisian Republic in 1956.

The Tunisian Revolution of 2011 overthrew President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 24 years in power and set off the wider Arab Spring. A new constitution was adopted on 26 January 2014, and a constitutional referendum in 2022 made it a unitary presidential republic.

The population is 12.1 million, the vast majority Arab and Muslim. Arabic is the official language, and French serves as an administrative and educational language without official status. The European Union is the first trading partner: Tunisia signed an Association Agreement with it in July 1995, the first Mediterranean country to do so.
turin: Turin lies in north-western Italy, mainly on the western bank of the River Po, surrounded on the west and north by the Alps and on the east by a high hill that continues the hills of Monferrato. Four major rivers pass through it: the Po and its tributaries the Dora Riparia, the Stura di Lanzo and the Sangone.

The Taurini, a Celto-Ligurian Alpine people, occupied the upper valley of the Po. In 218 BCE Hannibal, allied with their enemies the Insubres, took their chief town, Taurasia, after a three-day siege. In the 1st century BCE the Romans founded Augusta Taurinorum, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants within high walls; its Porta Palatina is still preserved. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was held by the Heruli, Ostrogoths and Lombards, and passed to the Franks under Charlemagne in 773. The Counts of Savoy gained control after the marriage of Adelaide of Susa to Otto, son of Humbert Biancamano, and when the city was annexed to the Duchy of Savoy at the end of the 13th century it had 20,000 inhabitants.

Emmanuel Philibert, nicknamed Iron Head, made Turin the capital of the Duchy of Savoy in 1563. The French Empire annexed it with the rest of Piedmont in 1802, and in 1814 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia was restored with Turin as its capital. That kingdom led the struggle for the unification of Italy, and Turin was the political and intellectual centre of the Risorgimento. It became the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861; the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome after the conquest of the Papal States in 1870.

Turin is the capital of Piedmont and is sometimes called the cradle of Italian liberty. Its architecture is predominantly Baroque, and part of the historical centre is inscribed in the World Heritage List as the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. It is the base of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo, and hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.
turkey: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia, which makes up 97% of its surface, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Together they cover 783,562 square kilometres, and the Turkish straits and the Sea of Marmara run between them. The inland Anatolian Plateau grows more rugged towards the east, where Mount Ararat, the highest point at 5,137 metres, and Lake Van, the largest lake, are found. The Euphrates, the Tigris and the Aras rise in the east, and the country is divided into seven major regions.

The area has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic and holds some of the oldest Neolithic sites, among them Göbekli Tepe, close to 12,000 years old, and Çatalhöyük. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The Hittite kingdom, with its capital at Hattusa, lasted approximately between 1700 and 1200 BCE, and Phrygia was established around 750 BCE. Alexander the Great's conquests brought Hellenization, followed by Romanization under the Roman and Byzantine empires.

The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243, after which Turkish principalities emerged. From 1299 the Ottomans united them, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The Ottoman state entered World War I in 1914, and its government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek and Assyrian subjects. After defeat came the Turkish War of Independence, the abolition of the sultanate and the Treaty of Lausanne. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first president, proclaimed the Republic on 29 October 1923.

Turkey has more than 86 million people. Most are ethnic Turks, and Kurds are the largest minority, with estimates ranging from 12 to 20% of the population because census figures have not recorded ethnicity since 1965. Ankara is the capital and Istanbul the largest city. The country is a presidential republic under the constitution approved by referendum in 1982, with a 600-member Parliament and 81 provinces.
turku: Turku lies at the mouth of the Aura River in the south-western corner of Finland and covers both banks. The eastern bank, where Turku Cathedral stands, is the older and original centre; the western side, with Turku Castle, is the newer part. South-western Finland stayed below sea level for a long time after the Ice Age, and tectonic uplift turned the region from an outlying archipelago into a shoreline between about 3000 and 2000 BCE. In the Iron Age it was densely populated, and the word Finland once referred only to the area round Turku, which is why the province is called Finland Proper.

The Finnish name Turku is related to the word torg, meaning market. Pope Gregory IX mentioned the town of Aboa in his bull of 1229, and that year is now used as the founding year of the city. By the pope's permission of 23 January 1229 the episcopal seat was moved from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near the present centre. Because no reliable document records the founding, it has also been suggested that the city was founded in the 1280s or 1290s by the joint initiative of the king, the bishop and the Dominican Convent of Saint Olaf. Turku was the most important city in Finland under Swedish rule.

After the Finnish War, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia at the Treaty of Fredrikshamn in 1809, and the Russians entered Turku in October 1809 without resistance. Turku became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland but lost the status in 1812, when Emperor Alexander I decided to move the capital to Helsinki. After the last great fire, in 1827, most government institutions were moved to Helsinki together with the Royal Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, which later became the University of Helsinki.

Turku is the oldest city in Finland and the regional capital of Southwest Finland, with about 210,000 inhabitants. It is officially bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Swedish-language Åbo Akademi was founded there in 1918 and the Finnish-language University of Turku two years later. Its port runs ferries to Stockholm and Mariehamn.
